articles.title: Spurring economic growth
articles.content: THE World Bank’s Reclaiming Momentum Towards Prosperity report presents a sobering reality: poverty has climbed back to 25.3 per cent on the national line; and close to 45pc of Pakistanis fall below the bank’s new $4.20-a-day threshold. Stabilising our way into deeper poverty has exposed the limits of conventional macroeconomic management. Speaking last week at the International Conference on Inclusive and Resilient Economic Empowerment and Growth, organised by the Pakistan Poverty Alleviation Fund in Islamabad, I put one question at the centre: how do we break this cycle? Accelerating growth requires recognising where real growth originates. Pakistan’s largest capital investment of this decade never appeared in a Public Sector Development Programme (PSDP), Annual Development Programme (ADP), or Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC). Farmers, shopkeepers and households imported about 17 gigawatts of solar panels in 2024, and the same again in 2025. No PC-1. No donor. No climate finance unit. They used their own savings, because diesel costs and the unwinding of unsustainable energy subsidies made it rational. The lesson for macroeconomic policy is direct. Prolonged, distorted subsidies are not a safety net. They are an obstacle to citizen-led growth. When fiscal pressure forced the state to pare them back, citizens moved faster than planners to protect their own balance sheets. The state’s response was to tax panel imports and revise net-metering terms. So when we ask how planning can accelerate growth, we should first admit that citizens are already ahead of the plan. The question is whether the state will remove the friction in their way or keep chasing donors. Three shifts would make the difference. Unpriced risk: Macroeconomic stability cannot survive risk that no one has priced. Pakistan already has a climate budget. It is not the one captured by the recently introduced climate budget tagging. It is the one written after each disaster. Major floods now produce post-disaster needs assessments, reconstruction budgets, and emergency appeals. That is our real climate expenditure: unplanned and largely borrowed — a permanent drag on fiscal space. The fix is not more tagging of development spending. It is pricing climate risk before it arrives. Pakistan already has a climate budget — the one written after each disaster. In practice, this means treating climate losses as a contingent liability of each province, the way we already treat circular debt and SOE guarantees. The Fiscal Risk Statement mentions disasters but puts no number on them. Each province can estimate its average annual loss from floods, heat, and drought, and appropriate a share of it every year as an expected cost. Budget theorists call this ‘expected-value budgeting’. A loss that is budgeted becomes a decision. A loss that is not budgeted becomes a bailout, often paid through the Benazir Income Support Programme’s emergency transfers. Maintenance first: Economic productivity depends on assets that work. That makes resilience a maintenance problem before it is a development problem. Embankments, drains, canals, and roads do not fail because nobody built them. They fail because their recurrent budgets are starved. Yet our economic conversation stays inside the development budget. The federal PSDP alone carries a throw-forward of about Rs11 trillion, and new schemes keep joining the queue, while existing assets go unmaintained. The ADP builds the embankment. The operations and maintenance line decides whether it holds. Protecting maintenance allocations for water assets would preserve existing capital and buy more resilience per rupee than most new projects. One can see where local money is actually spent. The most local spending stream is not an SDG-linked programme. It is the parliamentarians’ development schemes: tube-wells, link roads, drains, and culverts. They are quick, uncoordinated, and climate-blind. Nobody screens them. A single check asking whether the asset will survive the next monsoon would protect more local capital than every formal climate project combined. Green growth at the local level will not come from specialised projects. It will come when ordinary public spending stops creating new fiscal liabilities. District arithmetic: Growth targets fail when they stay abstract. The NDC is written in tonnes of carbon and gigawatts. A district plans in culverts, acres, and tube-wells. Nobody has done the translation. A union council cannot own or deliver a national target expressed in metrics it does not know. The first mechanism is a translation layer. Each district needs a short climate investment and growth plan that converts national targets into local units: acres under laser levelling and drip irrigation, tube-wells solarised, kilometres of drains cleared. Once a target is counted in local units, a local official can be held accountable for it. The second mechanism is money that rewards performance instead of rescuing failure. Versions of this model already work elsewhere. A district that sets up its own climate fund and meets basic public financial management standards qualifies for performance-based grants spent on investments its communities choose. Money follows institutions, not proposals. Pakistan could pilot this in 10 of its most flood-exposed districts through provincial finance commission transfers, with the grant rising as each district meets its conditions. That is local ownership with a test attached. The third mechanism is creditworthiness. Local growth stays dependent on donor projects because no district or municipal body can borrow or issue a municipal bond. None has a balance sheet, an asset inventory, audited accounts, or a credit rating. A provincial pooled financing facility could bundle bankable projects, such as solar for water supply, municipal waste, and cold storage, and raise capital against the pool. The precondition is unglamorous: audited accounts and own-source revenue at local level. Investors do not lend to plans. They lend to entities with a record. The fourth point is simpler. For most local investment, the bottleneck is not finance. It is permission. A solar mini-grid needs a Disco connection and a Nepra licence. A restoration project needs a land lease. A water scheme needs water rights. Locally owned investment needs a single district window for permissions before it needs another fund. In all: price the loss before the flood. Fund maintenance before new projects. Count targets in district units. Make municipalities bankable. Citizens have already shown, panel by panel, even when they are below the poverty line, that they will finance their own resilience. The state cannot lead them, but can stop taxing their initiative and carry the risks they cannot.
articles.author: Ali Tauqeer Sheikh

articles.title: Talking taxes
articles.content: IN the two days before writing this column, I had the pleasure of being immersed in a series of discussions in Islamabad on all things related to taxes in Pakistan. Hosted by the finance ministry and the IMF, the discussions brought together senior practitioners, advisers, and stakeholders for a detailed, high-level debate on what all needs to change in Pakistan’s tax system for it to play a more enabling role in undergirding stability for the private sector and promoting growth rather than being a drag on it. What struck me during the discussions was the large gulf between the community of experts the IFIs bring to the tax conversation and the people who legislate and oversee the making and implementation of tax policy in Pakistan. The gulf is evident in how they approach the question of tax, the priorities they bring to the table, how they measure success, and the language they use to talk about taxes. The experts present — sadly, the content of the discussions was “off the record”, so only broad themes can be discussed here — emphasised sustained commitment, balanced compliance, and measuring outcomes, “not activity”. Special emphasis was put on the harmonisation of GST, predictability of policy, and the mutually reinforcing dynamic between various tax heads — for example, how a properly administered GST can help strengthen income tax as well. FBR representatives underlined their tax reform efforts. However, participants still pointed out that the base remains narrow, that withholding plays an outsize role — one of the charts showed how 90 per cent of withholding taxes are collected under 10 heads only — and that this role is increasing. There was broad consensus that Pakistan’s tax system remains inequitable, riddled with “distortions”, and serves more as a drag on growth and investment than as their promoter. It is surprising how underdeveloped the template governing data disclosure on revenues is. There is a reason why this is so. The priorities that have shaped Pakistan’s tax system over the years differ from what tax experts suggest it should serve. In Pakistan, raw revenue is the metric of success — and not efficiency, buoyancy, or the self-reinforcing elements of tax administration. Tax policy responds heavily to voice in the system. Over the years, it has evolved along the path of least resistance, so to speak, causing the bulk of the burden of generating new revenue to fall on those with no voice, or the least organised voice, in the system. Even in the section of industry that likes to highlight the quantum of its contribution to the revenue effort, it is highly probable that the bulk of the taxes are passed through to their consumer base rather than being borne by the owners and controllers of capital. Over the years, this course has led to a tax system that is highly regressive, very concentrated, barely buoyant, and heavily reliant on withholding as the basis for its collection. As participants grappled with the vexing question of tax reform in Pakistan, I felt one modest but concrete proposal might help refocus the conversation on evidence rather than emotion. Given how central the question is to Pakistan’s economic future, it is surprising how underdeveloped the template governing data disclosure on revenues is. The monthly revenue collection data we all see reported in the newspapers is informally taken by reporters from unnamed FBR sources and is often inconsistent. We only see revenue-collection data when the Fiscal Operations data is released every quarter, but even then it provides only headline numbers, and its release frequency is too low to be useful. One thing that is sorely needed in Pakistan is a more robust, mandatory data release template for the FBR, with monthly frequency at the very least, if not more often. The IMF should use its access to the highest levels of government to urge that monthly data releases on revenue collection become mandatory for the FBR. The World Bank should offer its expertise to help develop this template, with uniform accounting conventions governing matters such as how to treat withheld refunds and how to break down the releases. Hence, they serve as a meaningful source for discerning the direction of the fiscal outlook during the fiscal year. The government should legislate this requirement and make any necessary modifications to FBR rules to ensure that a dedicated team is always at work within the tax authority, gathering, compiling, and preparing the next data release as per a predetermined schedule. While we’re at it, let’s also mandate a similar release requirement on the finance ministry on expenditures. Q Block already submits a monthly statement of all expenditures to the IMF, as per the accounting treatment given by the IMF itself. It would be relatively simple to make this public. There is no good reason not to do so. And many participants at the conference did point out that the question of revenue is connected to that of expenditure. The bad practices that characterise much of Pakistan’s tax system are a symptom of the environment in which tax policy is administered. That environment is riddled with discretionary powers whose sway in the tax bureaucracy is at the root of a lot of what ails the tax effort. The best antidote to discretionary powers is daylight, or transparency. Open a window. Let the light of day shine in the otherwise dark rooms in which the tax machinery is used to operating. Let them grow accustomed to the discipline a regular data-release template brings. Let them answer the questions that will naturally arise once the data starts to flow. And watch the tax conversation find the rails it needs to ride into the future. The writer is a business and economy journalist.khurram.husain@gmail.comX:@khurramhusain
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: The hollow prize
articles.content: NOTHING precious should be within reach of a vandal. In February 1845, the Portland Vase — a rare Roman cameo glass, dateable to the 1st century AD — was smashed into over 200 pieces by a drunken student. On May 21, 1972, in St Peter’s Basilica, Vatican City, Michelangelo’s priceless statue — the Pietà — was damaged by a deranged geologist, Laszlo Toth. It took Toth minutes to vandalise what had taken Michelangelo two years to sculpt. Specialists spent 10 months restoring 100 fragments to the statue, using marble removed from the back of the sculpture. Cruelly, the original tip of Mary’s nose could not be recovered as it had been pocketed by some unfeeling tourist. It has taken President Donald Trump less than two years to trivialise the Nobel Peace Prize, to lower it from distinction to ridicule. Alfred Nobel instituted his Peace Prize in 1901 in a belated act of contrition for having invented dynamite and ballistite. His ingenuity converted his Bofors manufactory into an arms producer. That brainchild, however, proved to be the undoing of the Congress party and its leader Rajiv Gandhi. The party lost the November 1989 general elections after the revelation that key Indian politicians and uniformed personnel had received over $6.5 million in bribes from Bofors. It has taken Trump less than two years to trivialise the Nobel Peace Prize. It is said that peace activist Bertha von Suttner, a friend of Nobel’s, persuaded him to institute a Peace Prize. Nobel died in 1896. Nine years later, Bertha received her friend’s Peace Prize “for her audacity to oppose the horrors of war”. Clearly, the politicisation of the prize began early. Over the past 125 years, the Peace Prize committee has deviated from Nobel’s intention — to honour those who had “done the most or the best work for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies and for the holding and promotion of peace congresses”. Individual awardees have outrun institutions. The Peace Prize committee has recognised more than 110 individuals and almost 30 organisations. The International Committee of the Red Cross has won three times (the last in 1963), and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees twice (in 1954 and 1981). Neither in this war-torn world has won since. Individuals include adversaries rewarded for signing blood-stained peace accords (Menachem Begin/Anwar Sadat in 1978, and in 1994 Yasser Arafat, Shimon Peres, and Yitzhak Rabin). In 1973, Henry Kissinger got it for halting his bombing of North Vietnam; his victim, the Vietcong leader Le Duc Tho, declined to accept the award or share the podium with his American nemesis. In 1993, a jailer, South African president F.W. de Klerk, was placed on a par with his former prisoner Nelson Mandela for “the peaceful termination of the apartheid regime”. Three leaders have received the award for “non-violent struggles” — Albert Luthuli in 1960; Martin Luther King Jr in 1964; and Aung San Suu Kyi in 1991. This year, again, the Nobel Peace Prize committee has refused to oblige Trump. It is galling for him to know that three of his predecessors received the Peace Prize — Woodrow Wilson in 1920 for ending World War I; Jimmy Carter in 2002 for finding “peaceful solutions to international conflicts”; and Barack Obama in 2009 for strengthening “international diplomacy and cooperation between peoples”. Trump, if he is to be awarded anything, should be given an inverted prize for starting wars. Most Nobel Laureates donate their prize money to charities or noble causes. Our own Nobel Laureate Malala Yousafzai has put her prize money of $500,000 to beneficial use. She and her enterprising father Ziauddin Yousafzai founded the Malala Fund in 2013 to champion “every girl’s right to 12 years of education”. The latest report of the Malala US Fund and Malala Fund Nigeria for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, reveals an amount of $53.6 million (up from $8m in 2025), with investments of another $30.6m (up from $28.4m the previous year). Additionally, she and her father have earned over $2m from their autobiographies. By comparison, the Edhi Foundation in Pakistan announced its annual surplus in 2024 at Rs5.1 billion and its net assets at Rs42bn. The Edhi Foundation in the US has about $30m in net assets and in the UK another £40m. For Trump, charity begins at home. Even though he is worth over $7bn, he remains infused with “self and vain conceit”, craving that “hollow crown/ That rounds the mortal temples” of Nobel winners. He is obviously not satisfied with the FIFA Peace Prize given to him in 2025 by the kowtowing FIFA President Gianni Infantino. That leaves Trump with only one option: he must persuade President Vladimir Putin to award him the Order of Lenin. The writer is an author.www.fsaijazuddin.pk
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Energy transition
articles.content: RENEWABLE energy systems have advanced at an unbelievable pace in the last three decades. On technological grounds, the progress has been undeniable. On social levels, acceptance has grown across continents. In larger economies like Germany and Denmark, wind and solar installations have multiplied. In developing countries across Asia and Africa, renewable projects have flourished. Pakistan is one of the best examples of solar uptake. It has penetrated metropolitan centres and agricultural communities in remote villages. The infrastructure has spread with remarkable speed. These systems have shown promise in multiple dimensions. They have contributed to energy security through distributed generation. Their transformative ability has appeared to be exemplary. They have nearly toppled the fossil economy and defied the bureaucratic red tape that once constrained energy projects. They have challenged the energy status quo and established power structures. The International Energy Agency, which was established in response to the oil crisis of the 1970s, has increasingly focused on renewable energy. In its 2025 report, it projected that renewable capacity would increase by 4,600 gigawatts between 2025 and 2030, equivalent to the combined power generation capacity of China, the European Union, and Japan. Hence, the renewable energy systems turned ‘arrogant’ — an arrogance rooted in their advances. It manifested in declarations about inevitable energy transitions. It emerged in confidence that renewable systems would simply displace conventional energy without negotiation. The sector spoke with the certainty of inevitable victory. The Hormuz crisis brought everyone back to the fossil fuel debate. But all this confidence was challenged when a new geopolitical reality intervened and the US-Iran tensions escalated into a war, with the Strait of Hormuz surfacing as a critical news highlight. Through a single narrow waterway controlling a significant share of global energy flows, the entire discourse around renewable energy vanished from the public consciousness. This brought everyone back to the fossil fuel conversation. The commitments that renewables had made to energy independence suddenly fell short. Their role, once heralded as transformative, appeared insufficient when energy security was actually threatened. Their prominence in the energy debate was overshadowed by the immediate need to secure oil and gas supplies. Their ability to replace conventional energy had been overestimated. This conflict proved something fundamental: the technological advances in renewable energy systems are not yet ready to eliminate the world’s dependence on fossil fuels. Renewable systems also depend on governmental decisions, infrastructure investments, and political priorities. They are unsafe in isolation and the industry is sensitive to geopolitical interests. Their success is conditional on the fossil fuel economy itself. What else has this war taught us? That energy transition cannot proceed through wishful thinking or technological optimism alone. The path forward requires cooperation between the fossil fuel economy and the emerging green economy. The latter has yet to demonstrate the ability to recognise that governments remain important actors, not obstacles. They hold real power in the equation that involves energy policy, infrastructure, and national security. Ideologies have relevance when they align with national interests. Policies have tangible influence on energy markets and security. The conversation around a ‘just transition’ must, therefore, be fundamentally refra- med. A just transition will not be born in a vacuum or exist as a parallel system operating independently. It cannot emerge from disconnected green economy initiatives alone. The green economy, as a parallel vertical operating separately from existing energy systems, is not sustainable. It is an approach that the geopolitical crisis has now exposed. Instead, genuine transition will be born through cooperation with the fossil fuel economy. Through negotiation, mutual interest, and acknowledgement of interdependencies. Through recognition that energy security remains a global concern that transcends ideological preferences. Through acceptance that the transition will be messier, slower, and more politically complicated than renewable advocates may have imagined. The Strait of Hormuz crisis delivered a necessary lesson in humility. Renewable energy remains important, but it is not yet the complete answer to energy security. The path forward requires not the triumph of one system over another, but rather the difficult work of integration and transition that respects both technological capacity and geopolitical reality.
articles.author: Umer Farooq

articles.title: Makkah pact clarity
articles.content: THERE had been much speculation about what exactly the trilateral Makkah Joint Defence Agreement entails, other than general commitments about the collective defence of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye. But with the release of thetextof the 16-article agreement, there is now some clarity about its objectives. While Article 2 says that an “externally originating armed attack” on any of the signatories will be considered an attack on all, triggering the right of self-defence under the UN Charter, the agreement is silent on offensive action. This should settle questions about the extent of involvement of the pact allies in the ongoing Saudi-Houthi war, and any future engagement. That it is a purely defensive arrangement was also echoed by the Turkish foreign minister. He stressed it was not an “offensive agreement”, and ruled out sending his country’s troops to a foreign theatre. Other salient features of the pact include joint defence production, intelligence sharing and the interoperability of forces. Such clarity is welcome. While the defence of Saudi Arabia is important, Pakistan, Turkiye, and other regional states should continue efforts to find a negotiated solution to the Yemen conflict — both between the Saudis and Houthis and within Yemen. In a related development, Pakistan’s chief of defence forces was inTehranon Tuesday to try and prevent further escalation on the war front. The message from Tehran is that the US should accept Iran’s seven-point proposal if talks are to restart. A key Iranian demand is a ceasefire on all fronts, the end of the American blockade, lifting of sanctions, and the release of the Islamic Republic’s funds. However, despite the efforts of Pakistan and others, there are troubling noises coming from Washington and Tel Aviv. The abrasive US war secretary — who is no proponent of peace and dialogue — was recently inIsrael, while the Israeli prime minister, who will be fighting for his political survival in next week’s elections, has said he and President Donald Trump need to ‘eliminate’ the “Iranian regime”. Even the sincerest effort to bring peace to the Gulf, Yemen, and the wider Middle East will come to naught if the US and Israel continue with their provocative behaviour. A strike on Iran after the Israeli and US elections would be a massive blunder, and if there are any mature advisers left in Washington, they should talk the US president out of making any such move, besides warning Tel Aviv against such arrogant action. Iran may be under pressure, but as the past several months have shown, it has the capacity to withstand considerable pain inflicted on it by the US and Israel. Fresh aggression can kick off a firestorm that will be in no one’s control, hence it is best to abandon such reckless plans.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Common ground
articles.content: IT appears that the PML-N, echoing the PPP’s recent offer, is also willing to re-engage with the opposition, at least on counterterrorism policy. Though that may seem like a narrow scope for dialogue, in our vitiated political environment, it does offer an opening. Whether the opposition is interested in taking it up is a different question. The anger over the dismissal of the elected PTI government in KP is still far from subsiding, and the ruling coalition in Islamabad deserves much of the blame for making a negotiated settlement more difficult than it seemed two weeks ago. That said, the opposition also needs to introspect. From the murmurings of resentment within its ranks, it appears that the outcome of its last round of discussions with the government was not what many were hoping for. Yet, its street agitation has delivered even less. An offer for dialogue, even if focused on counterterrorism strategy, is still an opportunity to return to the negotiating table and continue from where the last round of talks left off. Complete disengagement will achieve nothing. Regrettably, the two sides still fail to see the country’s economic, security, and governance crises as challenges that must be solved politically. A nation of 260m can hardly afford such paralysis. The greater onus lies with the government. It is difficult to see how a credible counterterrorism strategy can be framed when the province on the front line of the fight has just been deprived of its elected government. If Islamabad wants its offer to be taken seriously, it should pair it with a real gesture of good faith, starting with a meaningful voice for KP’s elected representatives in any talks. Yet the government seems consumed by the hubris of unchecked power, while the opposition, particularly the PTI, continues to act as if agitation alone can yield results. Instead of evading Pakistan’s challenges through constant jousting and whataboutery, the political leadership needs to confront its failings. Counterterrorism, where the stakes for KP are the highest and broad-based consensus is urgently needed, is as good a place as any to begin. But it must lead to a much wider conversation on national issues. If the two sides cannot find common ground even on the fight against terrorism, the public would be justified in wondering what, if anything, they are capable of agreeing on.
articles.author: Editorial
